scenes.title: Cold open
narration: The Bird Dance: A Night of Yuman Song
This is Bird Dance. Traditional.
on_screen: Title card: Bird Dance · USA · Traditional

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The Bird Dance is rooted in the traditions of Yuman tribes, including the Cocopa and Mohave.
Songs were traditionally learned through apprenticeship or inherited, sometimes through dreams.
The practice is documented in early 20th-century ethnographic studies of Yuman music.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: The dance is a nocturnal event that lasts all night.
It is deeply connected to Yuman cultural identity and oral history, with songs reflecting migration narratives.
Today it is a living tradition.
on_screen: Footage: Five Windows into Africa: a CD-ROM (2000) (https://archive.org/details/FiveWindowsIntoAfrica2000)

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Dancers, typically young women (1-5), stand in a row facing the singers.
The movement consists of moving backward and forward over a distance of about 15 feet.
The performance is nocturnal and follows a specific sequence of songs.
on_screen: Formation: Row of 1-5 women facing singers; 15-foot path.
scenes.music: diegetic (the video's own sound), underscore under narration

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The music is performed by a lead singer and helpers, all using gourd rattles.
The songs are sung in the 'old language' and follow a sequence that increases in volume throughout the night.
Listen for the Gourd rattle.
The pulse is 5-8 time noted for some songs.
The music is characterized by the sound of gourd rattles accompanying vocalists. Songs vary from near-monotones to those using ascending and descending minor thirds.
on_screen: Instrument names on screen as each is mentioned
Waveform or rhythm-pattern graphic: Syncopation is frequent; rattle rhythm is approximately in eighth notes.

scenes.title: A respectful note
narration: The Bird Dance is a traditional Yuman practice involving songs in an 'old language' and should be approached with respect for its cultural and historical significance to the Cocopa and Mohave people.
